en: Thus, those who were like the lords of the gods, the sons of those [lords] such as Bhīma and Sahadeva, heroes whose vows were unshaken, possessing the luster of the sun,
and with Keśava and Umā hidden within them— having seen that [world] in the hands of a worthy recipient, they did not undertake the mendicant’s life out of pity for the world.
Who is able to alter the lines of destiny well-known as being inscribed by the hand of the Creator upon the scroll of fate?

*Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.* I bow to that Knowledge, who is the embodiment of the nectar flowing from the bliss of the indivisible single essence, whose form is pure consciousness, and who is beautiful with bliss.

(1) Now I shall describe in detail the supreme method of recitation (*pārāyaṇa-vidhi*), by the mere understanding of which one becomes directly the Supreme Śiva. (2) [The nature of Time is ignorance...]

Even if one recites mantras for millions upon millions of times, success will not arise for him unless he applies himself to the mantras once his own [inner] accomplishment is attained. (3) Knowledge of the nature of Time and the calculation of the *ahargaṇa* (the sum of days elapsed since the beginning of the Kalpa) leads to the attainment of the Eightfold Path; this is not the fruit of mere minor austerity. (4) First, the *ahargaṇa* of the current Kalpa and so forth is stated therein, by which the attainment of the Eightfold Path becomes immediate. (5) The full [count] consists of the elapsed years multiplied by seven and added to the current year; they should be joined with those wearing new garments.

One should know the Śaka era to be multiplied by twenty-two and sixty, mixed with the elapsed years, and increased by nine, seven, and three (6). When sixty is completed, one should add one to the wheel-marks; by that very [method], the remainder is to be subtracted from its own essence as before (8). The elapsed Kali [years] joined with nine, seven, and one, increased by fifteen, and added to the [current] lunar fortnights starting from Madhura, [divided] by three, [and reduced] by thirty horses (720)— (Aligned for clarity: *śakavatsarāḥ* (6) Furthermore, one should know the time of the Śaka king as multiplied by twenty-two and sixty, mixed with the elapsed years, and increased by nine, seven, and three (7). When sixty is completed, one should add one to the wheel-marks; by that very [method], the remainder is to be subtracted from its own essence as before indeed (8). The elapsed Kali [years] joined with nine, seven, and one, increased by fifteen, and added to the [current] lunar fortnights starting from Madhura, [divided] by three, [and reduced] by thirty horses (720)—)
(9) To those [constants] added the secret fruit, joined with the qualities of the moon, increased by the lunar days, then threefold; eight, zero, and mountain-divided;
multiplied by seasons and tastes, the result diminished by the intercalary months. Furthermore, the Śaka year multiplied by nine, seven, and eight becomes the elapsed Kali;

multiplied by the sun (twelve) and joined with the elapsed months, it is then threefold; then added to the quotient divided by thirty-three, that [result] (10) is multiplied by the quotient divided by fifteen and joined with the elapsed lunar days, then diminished by three, eight, and mountains (seven).

In this manner, the year-group diminished by the quotient of six and a half [from the elapsed years] becomes the *gaṇa* for the day of Venus at the base. Furthermore, the Śaka year plus the elapsed time in *dhūsī* years is called the "years of the Kalpa.

The group of years from the beginning of the Kalpa, multiplied by eleven and joined with the intercalary months of Caitra, is established; it is increased by the quotient obtained by dividing by ninety-seven, and then joined with the intercalary months.

Multiplied by thirty and added to the days, it is doubled, multiplied by eleven, divided by three, and subtracted; thus the *ahargaṇa* for the day of Venus is produced, free from the years of the Kalpa.

Thus, by the perfected sages and experts in the Tantras, it has been clearly established that the *ahargana* (the accumulated count of days) here is obtained by dividing [the elapsed time] by seven, starting with Venus (*śukra*). (12) When divided by five, it is the *udaya*; by nine, the *navavāsara*; by sixteen, the sixteen known as the *tithis*; and those named *paryāya*.
(14) Similarly, when divided by thirty-six, it becomes the *uduyogaka*. When divided by the sequence of the seasons and Vedas (four) and horses (seven), i.e., 47, it is the *yugasaṃtati*. (15)

That remainder, divided by the full wings of the Gargas and horses (252), is the *parivṛtti*. The remainder, divided by the arrows, clouds, and arrows (505), gives the years; this is mixed with one (the current year).

(16) The remainder of the years, divided by six (the tastes), gives the months elapsed therein. From the sequence of the remaining months, the days are to be known; thus do the wise understand it. (17) In this way, the accomplishment of the eight-fold [calculation] from this is remembered as being for the specific time (*tātkālikī*). The accomplishment of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) and yoga is declared in the formal declaration (*saṃkalpa-vācana*). (18) The remainder is the eight-fold [calculation].

This should be known by the best among those who know the *pārāyaṇa*: the planets [are determined] from nine times the sun [plus one], and the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) from the sky-goers (*grahas*). (19) In this very way, there shall always be the full knowledge of the groups of days; having understood this, the illustrious one should perform the ritual application (*viniyoga*). (20) Furthermore: the group of days (*gaṇa*) is threefold; the remainder of seven and five [is the day];

the lords of the divisions (*varga*) are the lords of the rising days (*vārodaya*); and from these five divisions, liberation arises for the practitioners (*upāsakas*). (21) The group of days [is calculated as] limbs, fires, eyes, and full moons.

The *maṇḍalaka* is that which has been traversed; it is called a *yuga*. The remainder, divided by six and seven (*rasādrī*), is called a *samā*. The months are the vowels. From the remainder divided by six, there arise the elapsed days and letters, remembered as the six letters beginning with *a* and ending with *ṛ* (*agnivarṇāḥ*). Thirty-six days constitute a month; eight months constitute a year. A half-year (*ayana*) is said to consist of thirty-six [months], and likewise a *maṇḍala* and a *yuga*. The weekdays and the *ghaṭikās* are the daily [cycle]; beyond that follow the year, the month, the *yuga*, and the revolution (*parivṛtti*).

(25) "The sevenfold recitation (*saptapārāyaṇa*) has been declared; that is proclaimed as having eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*). Without this, if one applies [the mantra], the accomplishment of the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*) does not arise. (26) Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Count of Days and so forth in the Ritual of Recitation," in the *Śrīmat-Saubhāgyatantra*. Now, I shall describe the characteristics of the recitations (*pārāyaṇa*); by knowing these, the preeminent practitioner (*sādhakeṃdra*) shall attain all accomplishments (*siddhi*). They are the four-limbed (*caturaṅga*), the five-limbed (*pañcāṅga*), the eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*), and the twelve-limbed (*dvādaśāṅga*).

Having understood the sixteen-fold division in sequence, one who is devoted to the *pārāyaṇa* [should know]: (2) Having joined the three *tāras*, the root-vidyā, and the [cycles of] years, months, and days—this procedure known as the "four-limbed" (*caturaṅga*) bestows perfect accomplishment. (3) Encompassing the day, the weekday, the fortnight, the month, and the year, this five-limbed sequence (*pañcāṅga-krama*) is to be known; it was practiced by Mārkaṇḍeya and others. (4) The weekday, the *ghaṭikā*s, the daily [cycle], and likewise the year, month, and yuga—this is the sequence for the revolution (*parivṛtti*). (5) A...

The sequence of twelve limbs, as proclaimed in the *Ṣṭāṅgakrama* and worshipped by Bhṛgu and others, consists of: the day (*vāra*), the pair of ghaṭīs, the month, the fortnight, the syllable, the lunar date (*tithi*), the constant (*nitya*), the revolution (*parivṛtta*), the great yuga (*mahāyuga*), the full (*pūrṇa*), the variegated (*śavalmaka*), heaven (*diva*), the great revolution (*mahāparivṛta*), and so on. (6–7) Furthermore, there is the full (*pūrṇa*), the immediate (*sadya*), the variegated (*śavala*), the dwarf (*kharva*), and thereafter the Rāma; likewise the great revolution (*mahāparivṛti*) and the ultra-revolution (*atiparivṛti*). (8) [The sequence continues with] the great yuga (*mahāyuga*), the yuga, the year (*varṣa*), the month, the small month (*laghumāsaka*), the fortnight (*pakṣa*), the Vinatī, the river (*tīrtha*), and the eternal (*nityā*).

Raṃ-gha-ṭi-man in sequence (9). Thus, the conjunctions with the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-yoga*) and the *karaṇas* constitute the sixteen-fold limb, numbering twenty seeds, which always belong to the sixteen-fold [system] (10).

He who thus knows the five limbs in the rite of the *pārāyaṇa* shall, as a yogin, attain the Brahman-nirvāṇa; of this there is no doubt (11). Thus ends the second [chapter], titled "The Description of the Sequence of the Five Limbs" in the *Pārāyaṇa-vidhi* of the glorious *Saubhāgyatantra*. Now, I shall proclaim the lineage of the twenty seeds.

Having known that which is declared in the sixteen-fold ritual procedure, one shall attain perfection. (1) The letter *A* is indeed named Pūrṇa; the letter *Ṣa* is called Tyamha; the letter *Ha* is named Śavala; and *Kheṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Kharvaka. (2) The syllable *Klīṃ* is named Rāma; the letter *Ru* is the Great Enclosure (*mahāparivṛti*). The letter *U* is the Enclosure, and *Khaṃ* is said to be the Great Yoke (*mahāyuga*). (3) The letter *Ya* is the seed-syllable of the Yoke; they declare "Navāni" [to be the next]. The thirty-six letters beginning with *A* are the syllables of the years.
Sixteen months are said to consist of [sixteen] vowels; furthermore, the number of days in a month is proclaimed to be thirty-six.

The sequence of thirty-six days consists of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*. A wise person should apply all of these; now the "light month" (*laghumāsa*) is described. The three days of the bright fortnight—the fifth, the tenth, and the full moon—as well as those in the dark fortnight, constitute the sequential application of the *kalpas*. In the deficient [fortnights], there are two [days] each.

The enumeration of the syllables is now declared; among the remaining [days], this is the determination for each single month of the moving [cycle]. (8) Here, the determination of the fortnights, which is most wonderful, is also attained in due order; those [syllables] that bestow the fruits of the thirty lunar days in both the bright and dark fortnights shall be explained. (9) On the fifth, tenth, and full-moon days, one should always utter four syllables at a time according to the rule. (10) On the other days as well, one should utter two syllables at a time; such is the designation of the fortnight.
This has been composed by the wise. (11) Now, for the sake of perfecting the *pārāyaṇa*, I shall explain the designation of the days.

Those thirty-six letters beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Kṣa' are proclaimed as the "letters of the day" (*dinārṇa*) by those expert in the *pārāyaṇa*. (12) The Nityās correspond to the number of vowels;
they are established in the sixteen vowels. (13) Beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā, each of these sixteen is to be known according to the sequence of the cycles.

The drumbeat of the Three Treatises (14). Therefore, I shall explain the vowels and the initial letters of the nine consonant groups: one should point them out as *a, ḷ, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and ṣa* (15).

These are to be known as the nine days (*vārāḥ*), which correspond respectively to the nine lords (*navanātha*). They are: Prakāśa, Vimarśa, Ānanda, Jñāna (16), Satya, Pūrṇa, Svabhāva, Pratibha, and Ubhaga. Within the month, there are four cycles (*āvṛtayaḥ*) of these days (17).

Furthermore, sixty *ghaṭikās* are to be known in a day; thus, the division of the fifty *mātṛkās* becomes fivefold. (18) From that, the groups (*vargas*) bearing those names are produced. Having ascertained the letter [of the day] and the rising of its *ghaṭikās*, the wise one should count from the beginning of that day and then recite the group (*varga*). (19) Now, the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) will be described according to the sequence of the letters as well: the six [groups] beginning with the letter *ḷ* and ending with the letter *l*. (20)

I shall now describe the thirty yogic phonemes; their enumeration is like that of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras). (21) The enumeration of the yogas is proclaimed as beginning with *a* and ending with *na*; for the purpose of calculation, the consonants from *ka* onwards are repeated three times, making twelve [groups]. (22) These are clearly to be understood as the months and the sixteen limbs (*ṣoḍaśāṅga*). Now, I shall explain the determination of the seasons (*ṛtu*) for the sake of attaining success in recitation (*japa*). (23) [The seasons are] Śrīkarī, Mohinī, Kāminī, and Vimalā.

Hāriṇī, Bhrāmiṇī, Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Kumārikā—(24) these eight Śaktis should be known as bestowing great accomplishment in the rite of Japa and worship. Puṣpiṇī, Kumārī, Mohinī, Vimalā, (25) Jayinī, and Śrīkarī—these are the six Parvas in sequence. Puṣpiṇī lasts for a year and two months; Kumārikā lasts for one month and one day; (26) Mohinī lasts for one year and one day; and Vimalā lasts from the rising of a month until the rising of a year.

Through the two [days] of Jayinī and Dinodaya, there is Śrīkarī (27). Thus, there shall be a period of six years; henceforth I shall describe the drinking of Soma. A year, a month, a fortnight, or indeed a day of rising (28)—this is called "drinking of Soma" by the wise who know the Āgamas. A year, a day, a lunar day, a weekday, and likewise a month (29)—the conjunction of these five syllables is the recitation performed during a solar eclipse. It is said that from Kāmeśvarī up to Citrānanda is the Dakṣiṇāyana.

(30) Starting from Cicā and ending with Kāmeśvarī, this is also called the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), which bestows the attainment of knowledge (*jñānasiddhi*). (31) The Sun, Venus, the Moon, Ketu, Mars, Mercury, Rāhu, Jupiter, and Saturn are declared to be the planets (*graha*) of the reciters (*japī*). (32) Even month by month, the sequence of the four limbs (*caturaṅgi*) is to be understood; thus has the characteristic of the recitation (*japa*) for the sixteen limbs and so forth been fully explained. (33) [This was taught] by the Illustrious One according to the rule.

"Devote yourself to you, the method of *pārāyaṇa*"; thus has been briefly declared the determination of the five limbs (34). Having performed the ritual of the sixteen limbs, one should commence the recitation (*japa*), which is to be kept secret with effort and is higher than the highest (35). Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Succession of Seeds of the Sixteen Limbs and so forth," in the *Pārāyaṇa-vidhi* of the venerable *Saubhāgyatantra*. Now, the reality (*tattva*) at the conclusion of the *pārāyaṇa*...
The determination of the enumeration is now stated: first therein is the *Caturaṅgaka*, which bestows accomplishment; the second is that called *Nātha*; the third belongs to the *Cakreśīs*;

the fourth is the *Ghaṭipārāyaṇa*; the fifth is designated by the name [of the deity]; the sixth is the *Mantrapārāyaṇa*; the seventh is that called *Tattva*; the eighth is indeed that called *Nityā*;
the ninth begins with *Mātṛkā*; the tenth is called *Laghumāsa*; the eleventh shall be the *Pakṣa*; the twelfth is called *Tithinityā*, and therein is that called *Ṛtu*.

The thirteenth is the one named Rāśi; the fourteenth is known as Khaṭa; the fifteenth is remembered as Bhūti; and the sixteenth is known as Haṃsa. The eighteenth is Vaśinī, and the nineteenth is Yuganātha. The twentieth is called Mudrā, while the twenty-first is named Cakra. The twenty-second is known as Raśmi; the six parvas are designated as Niṣaṭ; the thirty-first is Somapāna, which is declared to be Pārāyaṇa; and the thirty-second belongs to Sarvamaṅgalā.

The thirty-first is known as Sūryoparāga, which bestows all auspiciousness and success; the thirty-second belongs to Citrā; the thirty-third is named Ramā; the thirty-fourth belongs to Bhuvanā; and the thirty-fifth belongs to Kāmeśī. This entire Pārāyaṇa causes delight to the whole world. The thirty-sixth is declared to be the supreme Pārāyaṇa known as Āmnāya, which is the refuge for all people and the most excellent among the dwellers of heaven—[the Pārāyaṇa of] Śrīmattripurasundarī.

(11) Thus has been briefly declared this Sūtra, which bestows the empire of oceanic bliss and is exceedingly difficult to obtain. These indeed are the Vidyā-pārāyaṇas, numbering according to the principles (tattva). (12) He who performs these in this world is liberated; of this there is no doubt. [Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Number of Pārāyaṇas," in the section on the Ritual of Pārāyaṇa within the Śrīmat Saubhāgyatantra. Now, the Vidyā-pārāyaṇa is described in brief.

Having known these, the lord of practitioners shall possess a graceful form. First, I shall describe here that which bestows success, the four-limbed [practice], which is the eternal foundation of all recitations (*pārāyaṇa*). One should utter the Root-Vidyā in sequence: *Tāra* (Om), *Vāk* (Aim), *Mana* (Hrīm), *Māyā* (Hrīm), and *Śrī* (Śrīm). Then, after the eight-syllabled mantra, one should utter the face-enclosure (*mukhavṛta*) as prescribed. Then, for the fourth of the recitations, one should utter the syllable *Parā* (Hsraum) joined with the sprout of the *Haṃsa* (Saḥ).

The wise know the sequence as *vaṃ*, *kra*, *ma*, *vi*, *du*, *ru*, *bu*, *dhāḥ*. (4) From the first groups [of consonants]—*a*, *ḷ*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *ṣa*—the first syllable is formed by the first letter;

the second syllable is from the second letter; the third consists of two letters; and the fourth consists of three letters. (5–6) Having thus understood this four-limbed [mantra], which is heavy according to the scriptures, one should first recite it and thereby attain all accomplishments. Now, O Lord, I shall explain the supreme *pārāyaṇa* as the second [part]; having uttered the *tritārā* and so forth, (7) [one should proceed].

Then, one should utter the root-vidyā and so forth, followed by Māyā and Ramā, and the previously mentioned groups [of consonants] separately in nine ways. (8) Then, beginning with Prakāśa and ending with Subhagā in sequence, according to the order of the mandalas, the mantra should be recited four times during the months. (9) Now I shall describe the third [method], which bestows happiness upon the mistresses of the wheels (*cakreśīs*): having uttered the three *tārās* and so forth, one should recite the root-vidyā and so forth in sequence. (10) At the end, having spoken "Parā," then "Tripurā," and thereafter "Cakreśvarī"...

"O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, who possesses the form of the *rī* [syllable], I worship Your venerable sandals"—thus one should utter this, ending with a prostration. This is declared to be the *pārāyaṇa* by the name of the Nine Mistress of the Wheels (*navacakreśvarī*).
Now, that *ghaṭi-pārāyaṇa* and its method are described here: these are the names of the five groups of letters (*pañcātyudayakāni*).

Among them, whichever letter rises on a given day, that first syllable should be used as the beginning; one should recite this first group of letters. At the end of the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should add the three *tāras* (the three *oṃ*s). Thus it ends.

Having uttered the *haṃsapada* preceded by the syllable *ṛṃ*, this constitutes sixty recitations. (15) This is known as the *ghaṭi-pārāyaṇa*; it is remembered that sixty [recitations] are to be performed at the morning twilight, at the end of the evening twilight, or at all three junctions of the day—so say the Tantrikas. (16) Therefore, I shall now describe the fifth, the *nāma-pārāyaṇa*. Therein, first, for the sake of qualification, one should perform the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and place the *mātṛkā* [syllables]. (17) Having uttered the three *tāra*s, the root-vidyā, the daily [mantra], and so forth in sequence, one should place the aforementioned [syllables] as before. I shall describe the placement of the *mātṛkā*. Now I shall describe the seventh form, which is *pārāyaṇa*. It is prescribed for the midday *saṃdhyā*, following the recitation of the *gāyatrī*. One should not install [it] otherwise; by reciting the remainder as before, one shall attain success. [Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Recitation of the Goddesses Ramā, Bhuvanā, and Kāmeśī," in the Ritual of Recitation (*pārāyaṇa-vidhi*) within the *Śrīmat-Saubhāgya-tantra*. Now, the *Āmnāyas*...

The *Pārāyaṇa*, the foremost among the Bhidhas, is proclaimed; by knowing which, one becomes equal to Śiva in the Kali age without delay. (1) Śuddhavidyā, Chācābalā, Dvādaśārdhā, Ahasantika, Mātaṅgī, Śukaśārī, Vīṇā, and likewise Veṇu; (2) Laghuśyāmā, Samayā—these are the eleven [deities] of the former [group]. Saubhāgyavidyā, Bagalā, Vārāhī, and likewise Vaṭuka; (3) Tira... [the rest of the text follows].

In the Southern tradition, six [deities] are proclaimed: Lopaāmudrā, Bhuvanā, Aṃnapūrṇā, Mahākamā, and the goddess Kalā, along with Sanayāmbā; these five have been clearly established by those who know the Tantras as the Western Āmnāya. Then follow Turyāmbā, Mahārdhā, Śvārūḍhā, Miśrī, Vāgvādini, and Samayā—these six are likewise in the Northern [tradition]. [And] the venerable Mahāṣo...

The Ḍāśī-vidyā, the Parā-Ṣoḍaśikā, likewise the Parā-prāsāda-vidyā, the Parā-bhaṭṭārikā, the Parā-vāśā-bhavī-devī, the Anuttara-parāmbikā, the goddess Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, and Samaya— these eight in number are declared in the Urdhva-nāḍī by the best among those who know the Pārāyaṇa. Thus, all together, there is a lineage of thirty-six mantras in the *dinārṇa*.

One should apply oneself to the maṇḍala every month (9), and to each single day one by one, according to the sequence of the goddesses of the letters; therein, the distinction should be understood as beginning with the stars and the [deities] of the directions (10). This continuous succession, which encompasses the knowledge of the letters and the mouth-veil, is proclaimed as the Pārāyaṇa known by the tradition of the Āmnāya.
When preceded by the thirty-six [principles], it bestows the great sovereignty of Śiva upon the pure-souled one who has received prior consecration.

One who has received this from the mouth of the Guru and practices its service with devotion becomes the supreme qualified person. He who thus performs the recitation (*japa*) through the sequence of the *Pārāyaṇa* with devotion—while the measures (*māna*) are being maintained—he is truly the Supreme Śiva himself. [Thus ends the section on the Description of the Vedic Traditions (*Āmnāya-nirūpaṇa*) within the Ritual of the *Pārāyaṇa* in the glorious *Saubhāgyatantra*.]
The eleventh chapter. Homage to the venerable Rājarājeśvarī.
